newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algiers on high alert over bombs.
newsitem.headline: Algiers on high alert over bombs.

text.p: The Algerian capital Algiers, rocked by a rash of bombings, sent hundreds more plainclothes police into the streets to try to thwart more attacks by Moslem fundamentalists, residents said on Thursday.

Parents urged their children to steer clear of the city centre and security forces tightened up a ban on cars stopping in the city, preventing drivers from leaving them even for a short while, said residents speaking by telephone from Algiers.
"Obsessive fear grips Algiers and surrounding towns," wrote Liberte newspaper on Thursday, summing up the mood of Algiers's population of about four million people.
Young people set up a discreet vigil on street corners scrutinising drivers to try to keep their neighbourhoods free from bomb attacks, they added.

A huge car bomb exploded on Tuesday evening in central Algiers, killing 13 people and wounding at least 100, according to hospital sources. Security officials had said seven people were killed and more than 40 wounded in the city blast.
It was the third car bomb attack in the city within less than two weeks. Two car bomb explosions killed at least 18 people late in December.
El Watan newspaper reported on Wednesday that security forces had defused in the past week about 17 devices and cars laden with explosives set to explode in Algiers and surrounding towns.
Residents said on Thursday security forces had defused at least two car bombs on Wednesday in Madania district, not far from the presidential palace on the height of Algiers.
"People are more concerned and watchful of any suspicious car or objects around them because the bombs threaten everyone's life," said one resident who asked not to be named.
"My wife, my two children and myself cheated death last Tuesday as we passed by the blast spot one half hour before the bombing."

El Watan said a 27-year-old Moslem guerrilla, Farid Hamani, alias Abu Salmane, was the mastermind of the bombings and that he warned in a New Year's eve statement that the guerrillas had prepared about 50 bombs to be detonated in Algiers.
The newspaper identified Hamani as an Armed Islamic Group (GIA) leader in Algiers.
The rash of bombings and rebel attacks came ahead of the Moslem holy month of Ramadan.
Guerrillas, believing that the Ramadan fasting month is more fit for their "holy war", have stepped up their attacks during this month in the past four years in Algeria.
Ramadan is expected to start on Friday or Saturday in Algeria.

More than 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence pitting government forces against Moslem fundamentalists since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
